stem: Which feature makes an optimisation problem a linear program?
correct: The objective and all the constraints are linear functions of the decision variables.
A linear objective optimised under linear constraints and nothing more.

distractors.text: The decision variables are restricted to take only integer values.
distractors.misconception: confuses LP with integer programming

distractors.text: The objective contains a product of two decision variables somewhere.
distractors.misconception: a product term makes the objective quadratic

distractors.text: The feasible set must contain exactly one point for the problem to be solved.
distractors.misconception: confuses a feasible set with a unique solution

distractors.text: Every coefficient in the objective and constraints has to be positive.
distractors.misconception: invents a sign restriction on the data

distractors.text: All the constraints must be written as equalities and never as inequalities.
distractors.misconception: inequalities are allowed in an LP

explanation: Linearity of the objective and constraints is what defines an LP; integrality, products of variables or sign conditions on the data are separate matters.

stem: Which statement about the feasible region of a linear program is always true?
correct: It is convex: the segment between any two feasible points stays inside the region.
It is an intersection of half-spaces, so it is convex.

distractors.text: It is bounded whenever the optimal objective value of the LP is finite.
distractors.misconception: a finite optimum can occur on an unbounded region

distractors.text: It always has a non-empty interior, so a strictly feasible point exists.
distractors.misconception: the region can be a single point or a segment, or empty

distractors.text: It can consist of several disconnected pieces if the constraints conflict.
distractors.misconception: a set cut out by half-spaces cannot be disconnected

distractors.text: It always contains the origin once all variables are required to be non-negative.
distractors.misconception: ignores constraints of the form at least a positive number

distractors.text: It is always a bounded polygon with finitely many corner points.
distractors.misconception: regions can be unbounded or have no corner at all

explanation: Intersections of half-spaces are convex. The region can be unbounded, degenerate or empty, and need not contain the origin.

stem: A linear program has at least one vertex in its feasible region and has an optimal solution. What follows?
correct: At least one vertex of the feasible region is an optimal solution.
Some optimal solution is attained at a corner point.

distractors.text: Every optimal solution must itself be a vertex of the region.
distractors.misconception: ties along an edge give optimal points that are not vertices

distractors.text: The optimum can lie in the interior only when all objective coefficients are positive.
distractors.misconception: a linear objective never has an interior-only optimum without being constant along an edge

distractors.text: A vertex is optimal only when the optimal solution is unique.
distractors.misconception: a vertex can be optimal even when alternative optima exist

distractors.text: The gradient of the objective vanishes at the optimal point.
distractors.misconception: the objective gradient is a nonzero constant for an LP

distractors.text: Every point of the feasible region has the same objective value.
distractors.misconception: confuses optimality with a constant objective

explanation: A linear function attains its optimum at an extreme point; if the objective is parallel to an edge, the whole edge is optimal, but its end vertices are optimal too.

stem: In the graphical method, an objective contour line is parallel to a binding constraint and touches the feasible region along that edge at the optimum. What happens?
correct: Every point on that edge is optimal, so there are infinitely many optimal solutions.
The LP has alternative optima along the entire edge of the region.

distractors.text: The LP is unbounded because the objective can be improved without limit.
distractors.misconception: confuses alternative optima with unboundedness

distractors.text: The LP is infeasible because the contour line never meets the region.
distractors.misconception: the contour does touch the region

distractors.text: The optimum is unique and sits at the lower vertex of that edge.
distractors.misconception: assumes uniqueness despite the tie

distractors.text: The optimal objective value is zero because the contour passes through the origin.
distractors.misconception: invents a link between parallelism and a zero value

distractors.text: The LP has no optimal solution because the contour never leaves the region.
distractors.misconception: the optimum is attained on the edge

explanation: When the objective has the same direction as a constraint normal, moving along the edge does not change the objective, so all of its points are optimal.

stem: A feasible region of a two-variable LP is unbounded. Which conclusion is correct?
correct: The LP can still have a finite optimum, depending on the direction of the objective.
Boundedness of the LP depends on the objective direction too.

distractors.text: The LP is necessarily unbounded, with no optimal solution at all.
distractors.misconception: confuses unbounded regions with unbounded objectives

distractors.text: The LP must be infeasible, since a bounded region is required for a solution.
distractors.misconception: treats boundedness as necessary for feasibility

distractors.text: The optimum can only be found by moving to a point at infinity.
distractors.misconception: ignores that a vertex can be optimal

distractors.text: The optimal solution, if it exists, is never at a vertex.
distractors.misconception: an unbounded region can still have an optimal vertex

distractors.text: The optimal solution, if it exists, lies at the origin of the two variables.
distractors.misconception: invents a location for the optimum

explanation: For example, minimising $x+y$ over $x,y\ge0$ has a finite optimum although the region is unbounded; maximising it is unbounded.

stem: What is a basic feasible solution of $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$, where $A$ is $m\times n$ with rank $m$?
correct: Set $n-m$ variables to zero and solve for the other $m$, which must be non-negative.
A feasible point on linearly independent columns.

distractors.text: Any feasible point in which every component is strictly positive.
distractors.misconception: such a point is interior, not basic

distractors.text: A feasible point that maximises the objective function over the region.
distractors.misconception: confuses basic with optimal

distractors.text: A solution in which all $m$ basic variables are equal to zero.
distractors.misconception: that is the degenerate extreme case, not the definition

distractors.text: A feasible point in which every slack variable is equal to zero.
distractors.misconception: confuses basic solutions with points on every constraint boundary

distractors.text: A feasible point with at least one slack variable strictly positive.
distractors.misconception: slack positivity is unrelated to basic status

explanation: Fixing $n-m$ nonbasic variables at zero leaves a square system for the basis; the solution is a BFS if the basic values are non-negative.

stem: How are basic feasible solutions related to the geometry of the feasible region of an LP in standard form?
correct: They are exactly the extreme points (vertices) of the feasible region of the LP.
Each BFS is a corner of the feasible polyhedron, and conversely.

distractors.text: They are the points lying anywhere on the boundary of the feasible region.
distractors.misconception: boundary points include non-vertex points on edges

distractors.text: They are the intersections of constraint lines, whether or not these are feasible.
distractors.misconception: ignores that a basic solution may have negative components

distractors.text: They are interior points where all the slack variables are positive.
distractors.misconception: interior points are not extreme

distractors.text: They are only the optimal points, and any other vertex is not basic.
distractors.misconception: every vertex is a BFS, not only the optimal one

distractors.text: They correspond to the centroids of the faces of the feasible set.
distractors.misconception: invents a geometry unrelated to extreme points

explanation: A basic solution is any solution of a basis system; it is feasible only when all components are non-negative, and BFSs are exactly the vertices.

stem: In a maximisation problem, which nonbasic variable is the usual candidate to enter the basis under the largest-coefficient (Dantzig) rule?
correct: The one with the largest positive reduced cost, that is, the fastest rate of improvement.
The nonbasic variable with the largest positive $c_j-z_j$.

distractors.text: The variable that gives the smallest ratio in the minimum ratio test.
distractors.misconception: confuses the entering rule with the ratio test used for leaving

distractors.text: The basic variable that currently has the largest value in the solution.
distractors.misconception: mixes basic variables with the entering choice

distractors.text: The variable with the largest coefficient in the original constraint with the smallest right-hand side.
distractors.misconception: invents a rule based on constraints

distractors.text: Always the slack variable belonging to the tightest constraint.
distractors.misconception: slack variables are not always the entering choice

distractors.text: The nonbasic variable with the smallest current value in the solution.
distractors.misconception: nonbasic variables are all zero

explanation: Entering choice depends on reduced costs; the leaving choice, taken afterwards, comes from the ratio test.

stem: What is the purpose of the minimum ratio test in a simplex iteration?
correct: It selects the leaving variable, keeping every basic variable non-negative.
It finds how far the entering variable can grow.

distractors.text: It selects the entering variable that gives the greatest increase in the objective.
distractors.misconception: confuses the ratio test with the entering rule

distractors.text: It checks whether the current basic solution is optimal.
distractors.misconception: optimality is judged by reduced costs

distractors.text: It produces the dual solution associated with the current tableau.
distractors.misconception: the dual comes from reduced costs of slacks, not the ratio test

distractors.text: It guarantees that no basic variable can ever equal zero at a vertex.
distractors.misconception: ties in the test cause degeneracy rather than prevent it

distractors.text: It decides when the algorithm may stop because the objective stops changing.
distractors.misconception: stopping is decided by reduced costs

explanation: The ratio test finds the first basic variable to reach zero as the entering variable grows; that variable leaves, preserving feasibility.

stem: At optimality of a maximisation problem written in tableau form, which condition characterises the current basis?
correct: No nonbasic variable has a positive reduced cost at a feasible basis.
Every nonbasic reduced cost $c_j-z_j$ is non-positive.

distractors.text: Every basic variable is strictly positive and every slack variable is zero.
distractors.misconception: confuses optimality with non-degeneracy

distractors.text: All reduced costs of the nonbasic variables are strictly positive.
distractors.misconception: positive reduced costs mean the objective can still improve

distractors.text: The minimum ratio test produces a tie between two rows.
distractors.misconception: ties signal degeneracy, not optimality

distractors.text: The current objective value is equal to zero in the tableau.
distractors.misconception: optimal value need not be zero

distractors.text: The reduced costs of the basic variables are all strictly negative.
distractors.misconception: reduced costs of basic variables are zero

explanation: If no nonbasic variable has a positive reduced cost, increasing any of them cannot improve the objective, so the BFS is optimal.

stem: In the ratio test, only rows with a positive entry in the entering column are considered. Why?
correct: A non-positive entry means that basic variable does not decrease, so it gives no limit.
Such a basic variable never reaches zero as it grows.

distractors.text: Rows with a negative entry would make the current solution infeasible.
distractors.misconception: the current solution is feasible whatever the column entries are

distractors.text: Positive entries are the only ones that can be used to scale a row to 1.
distractors.misconception: confuses the pivot-scaling step with the test

distractors.text: A negative entry means the entering variable should be replaced by another one.
distractors.misconception: this changes the entering choice, which the test does not do

distractors.text: Rows with a zero right-hand side must be ignored for every choice of entering variable.
distractors.misconception: mixes the test with a degeneracy rule

distractors.text: A zero entry in the column makes the pivot element equal to one.
distractors.misconception: the pivot scaling is unrelated to the test

explanation: If all entries in the entering column are non-positive, nothing blocks the entering variable and the LP is unbounded.

stem: When is a basic feasible solution called degenerate?
correct: When at least one of the basic variables is equal to zero at that vertex.
Some basic variable takes the value zero there.

distractors.text: When some nonbasic variable is strictly positive in the solution.
distractors.misconception: nonbasic variables are zero by definition of a basic solution

distractors.text: When the LP has more than one optimal solution.
distractors.misconception: degeneracy and alternative optima are different phenomena

distractors.text: When no feasible solution exists for the constraint system.
distractors.misconception: confuses degeneracy with infeasibility

distractors.text: When all the reduced costs of the nonbasic variables are exactly zero.
distractors.misconception: zero reduced costs signal alternative optima

distractors.text: When two different constraints are parallel in the feasible region.
distractors.misconception: parallel constraints are not degeneracy

explanation: In a degenerate BFS more than $n-m$ of the variables are zero, so more constraints than needed are tight at the vertex.

stem: Which risk does degeneracy bring to the simplex method?
correct: Pivots can leave the objective unchanged, and the method may cycle forever.
Zero-step pivots may repeat; Bland's rule prevents it.

distractors.text: The LP becomes unbounded as soon as one basic variable equals zero.
distractors.misconception: degeneracy has no effect on boundedness

distractors.text: The objective value must increase strictly at every single pivot.
distractors.misconception: the opposite: degenerate pivots do not increase it

distractors.text: The optimal solution is no longer a vertex of the feasible region.
distractors.misconception: a degenerate vertex is still a vertex

distractors.text: The dual of the problem becomes infeasible at the degenerate point.
distractors.misconception: degeneracy does not affect dual feasibility in this way

distractors.text: The dual of the problem is guaranteed to be degenerate as well.
distractors.misconception: degeneracy of the primal does not force the dual to be degenerate

explanation: A degenerate pivot has step length zero, so the objective stays the same and the same basis can recur; Bland's rule prevents cycling.

stem: In a maximisation problem, how does the simplex method reveal that the LP is unbounded?
correct: An entering column has no positive entry, so the ratio test gives no limit.
The entering column is entirely non-positive.

distractors.text: A basic variable becomes negative after a pivot.
distractors.misconception: the ratio test prevents negative basic variables

distractors.text: Every reduced cost is non-positive in the optimal tableau.
distractors.misconception: that is the optimality test, not unboundedness

distractors.text: Every entry of the entering column is positive and the ratios are all equal.
distractors.misconception: equal ratios cause degeneracy

distractors.text: The Phase I objective stays positive at its optimum.
distractors.misconception: that signals infeasibility, not unboundedness

distractors.text: Every reduced cost becomes exactly zero after the pivot.
distractors.misconception: zero reduced costs signal alternative optima

explanation: With no blocking row the entering variable can increase indefinitely while the objective keeps improving.

stem: What is Phase I of the two-phase simplex method used for?
correct: It finds a feasible basis, or shows there is none, via artificial variables.
It produces a feasible starting basis for Phase II.

distractors.text: Computing the optimal solution of the dual of the original problem.
distractors.misconception: the dual is not computed in Phase I

distractors.text: Checking whether the original LP has a bounded objective.
distractors.misconception: boundedness is detected during Phase II

distractors.text: Maximising the original objective while ignoring all the constraints.
distractors.misconception: the constraints are kept in Phase I

distractors.text: Removing degeneracy from the starting tableau before pivoting.
distractors.misconception: degeneracy is not the point of Phase I

distractors.text: Checking that the artificial variables have no effect on the objective.
distractors.misconception: artificial variables are central to Phase I

explanation: Artificial variables give an easy starting basis; Phase I drives them to zero, giving a BFS for Phase II.

stem: Phase I ends with a strictly positive optimal value of the sum of artificial variables. What does this mean?
correct: The original LP is infeasible: the artificial variables cannot all be driven to zero.
No feasible point exists for the original constraints.

distractors.text: The original LP is unbounded and has no finite optimal solution.
distractors.misconception: confuses infeasibility with unboundedness

distractors.text: The original LP has an optimal solution, with some artificial variable kept positive.
distractors.misconception: a positive artificial variable violates the original constraints

distractors.text: Phase II should now be started with the artificial variables kept in the basis.
distractors.misconception: Phase II needs a feasible basis without them

distractors.text: The LP has multiple optimal solutions, so Bland's rule should be applied.
distractors.misconception: confuses with alternative optima

distractors.text: All artificial variables are zero, so Phase II can start from that basis.
distractors.misconception: gives the opposite outcome

explanation: A positive Phase I optimum means every point violates some constraint; the original problem is infeasible.

stem: What is the dual of the problem: maximise $c^\top x$ subject to $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$?
correct: Minimise $b^\top y$ subject to $A^\top y\ge c$ with non-negative $y$.
A minimisation with objective $b^\top y$, $A^\top y\ge c$, $y\ge0$.

distractors.text: Minimise $b^\top y$ subject to $A^\top y\le c$ and $y\ge0$.
distractors.misconception: gets the direction of the dual constraints wrong

distractors.text: Minimise $c^\top y$ subject to $Ay\ge b$ and $y\ge0$.
distractors.misconception: swaps the roles of $b$ and $c$ without transposing the matrix

distractors.text: Maximise $b^\top y$ subject to $A^\top y\ge c$ and $y\ge0$.
distractors.misconception: keeps the maximisation instead of switching to minimisation

distractors.text: Minimise $b^\top y$ subject to $A^\top y=c$ with $y$ free in sign.
distractors.misconception: that is the dual of an equality-form primal

distractors.text: Maximise $c^\top y$ subject to $A^\top y\le b$ and $y\le0$.
distractors.misconception: mixes the sign conventions of both problems

explanation: The dual has one variable per primal constraint and one constraint per primal variable; max with $\le$ constraints becomes min with $\ge$ constraints.

stem: Let $x$ be primal feasible and $y$ dual feasible for a maximisation primal $\max c^\top x$ and its dual. What does weak duality state?
correct: $c^\top x\le b^\top y$ for every feasible pair.
Dual values bound primal values from above.

distractors.text: $c^\top x\ge b^\top y$ for every such pair.
distractors.misconception: reverses the inequality

distractors.text: $c^\top x=b^\top y$ for every pair of feasible solutions.
distractors.misconception: equality only holds at optimality

distractors.text: $c^\top x\le b^\top y$ only when both solutions are optimal.
distractors.misconception: weak duality needs only feasibility

distractors.text: $c^\top x\le b^\top y$ only if the primal has a unique optimum.
distractors.misconception: adds a nonexistent uniqueness condition

distractors.text: $c^\top x\le b^\top y$ only when $A$ is a square matrix.
distractors.misconception: weak duality needs no assumption on the shape of $A$

explanation: Weak duality holds for all feasible pairs. In particular, a feasible pair with equal objective values is optimal for both problems.

stem: The primal LP has a finite optimal value. What does strong duality say about its dual?
correct: The dual also has an optimal solution, and its optimal value is the same.
Both problems attain the same optimal objective value.

distractors.text: The dual is unbounded and so has no finite optimal value.
distractors.misconception: unbounded dual would contradict weak duality

distractors.text: The dual optimal value is strictly smaller than the primal optimal value.
distractors.misconception: there is no duality gap in LP

distractors.text: The dual optimum is attained at the same vector as the primal one.
distractors.misconception: primal and dual solutions live in different spaces

distractors.text: The dual is infeasible, since only one of the pair can be feasible.
distractors.misconception: confuses with the unbounded-primal case

distractors.text: The dual has a feasible solution but no optimal solution.
distractors.misconception: weak duality guarantees a bound on feasible solutions

explanation: For LPs there is no duality gap: if either problem has a finite optimum, so does the other, with equal values.

stem: A maximisation LP is unbounded. What can be said about its dual?
correct: The dual problem has no feasible point at all.
No feasible solution exists for the dual.

distractors.text: The dual is unbounded as well.
distractors.misconception: weak duality would be violated by an unbounded pair

distractors.text: The dual has a finite optimum that equals zero.
distractors.misconception: a finite dual optimum forces a finite primal optimum

distractors.text: The dual may or may not be feasible, depending on the vector $b$.
distractors.misconception: weak duality forces infeasibility

distractors.text: The dual is feasible but has no optimal solution.
distractors.misconception: a feasible dual would bound the primal

distractors.text: The dual is feasible, but its objective is unbounded below.
distractors.misconception: weak duality would be violated by a finite feasible primal bound

explanation: A feasible dual point would give a finite upper bound on the primal objective by weak duality, contradicting unboundedness.

stem: The primal LP is infeasible. Which statement about its dual is correct?
correct: The dual is infeasible or unbounded.
No finite optimum for the dual.

distractors.text: The dual must be unbounded.
distractors.misconception: both the primal and the dual can be infeasible

distractors.text: The dual must be infeasible.
distractors.misconception: the dual can be unbounded

distractors.text: The dual has a finite optimal value equal to zero.
distractors.misconception: a finite dual optimum would force a primal optimum

distractors.text: The dual is feasible and bounded below.
distractors.misconception: strong duality would then give a feasible primal

distractors.text: The dual must have the same feasibility status as the primal.
distractors.misconception: an infeasible primal can have an unbounded dual

explanation: If the dual had a finite optimum, strong duality would give a primal optimum; so the dual is infeasible or unbounded (both cases occur).

stem: What do the complementary slackness conditions state for optimal $x^*$ and $y^*$ of a primal-dual pair?
correct: A positive variable forces the paired constraint to be tight.
For each pair, the variable is zero or its constraint is tight.

distractors.text: Every constraint of both problems must hold with equality at the optimum.
distractors.misconception: only constraints paired with positive variables must be tight

distractors.text: If a constraint has slack, its dual variable must be strictly positive.
distractors.misconception: reverses the implication

distractors.text: The vectors $x^*$ and $y^*$ are orthogonal to each other.
distractors.misconception: they live in different spaces

distractors.text: Primal and dual optimal solutions are equal vectors.
distractors.misconception: the two vectors have different meanings and sizes

distractors.text: The cost per unit of the resource, set by the market and independent of the model.
distractors.misconception: shadow prices come from the optimal dual

explanation: $x_j^*(A^\top y^*-c)_j=0$ and $y_i^*(b-Ax^*)_i=0$; a positive shadow price means the resource is fully used.

stem: What does the shadow price of a constraint measure?
correct: The change in the optimal value per extra unit of the right-hand side, in its range.
The marginal value of one more unit of the scarce resource.

distractors.text: The total amount of the resource used up by the optimal solution.
distractors.misconception: confuses a price with consumption

distractors.text: The amount of slack remaining in the constraint at the optimum.
distractors.misconception: confuses with the slack variable

distractors.text: The change in the objective per unit increase of a decision variable.
distractors.misconception: that is an objective coefficient or reduced cost

distractors.text: The price at which the resource can be bought, whatever its marginal value.
distractors.misconception: confuses with market price

distractors.text: A positive reduced cost of every nonbasic variable.
distractors.misconception: the sign pattern of reduced costs in the optimum is non-positive for a maximum

explanation: It is the optimal dual variable. It is valid only while the right-hand side stays within its allowable range.

stem: A constraint is not binding at the optimum of a maximisation LP. What is its shadow price?
correct: Zero, because extra resource would not improve the optimum.
Its dual value is zero by complementary slackness.

distractors.text: Positive, because every constraint has some value attached.
distractors.misconception: a slack resource is worth nothing at the margin

distractors.text: Equal to the amount of slack in the constraint.
distractors.misconception: confuses the price with the slack

distractors.text: Negative, since relaxing the constraint lowers the objective.
distractors.misconception: relaxing a constraint cannot lower a maximum

distractors.text: Equal to the objective coefficient of the variable using the resource.
distractors.misconception: mixes prices with objective coefficients

distractors.text: Undefined, because the constraint plays no role in the dual problem.
distractors.misconception: the dual variable exists and equals zero

explanation: If the constraint has slack, small changes of its right-hand side do not change the optimal solution, so its dual variable is $0$.

stem: What does the allowable range of a right-hand side $b_i$ describe?
correct: Values keeping the current optimal basis feasible, so the shadow price holds.
Values of $b_i$ for which the same basis stays feasible.

distractors.text: The interval over which the optimal values of the decision variables do not change.
distractors.misconception: the variable values do change with the right-hand side

distractors.text: The interval where the problem remains degenerate at the optimum.
distractors.misconception: degeneracy is unrelated to the range

distractors.text: The interval over which the objective value stays constant.
distractors.misconception: the objective value changes linearly with the shadow price

distractors.text: The interval where every reduced cost remains exactly zero.
distractors.misconception: reduced costs of nonbasic variables need not be zero

distractors.text: The interval over which the shadow price of the constraint keeps changing.
distractors.misconception: the shadow price is constant inside the range

explanation: Within the range the optimal basis is unchanged, the optimum moves linearly with $b_i$ at slope equal to the shadow price; outside it a different basis is optimal.

stem: The cost coefficient $c_j$ of a basic variable is changed within its allowable range. What happens to the optimal solution?
correct: The same vertex stays optimal, although the optimal value changes.
The variable values stay put while the objective value moves.

distractors.text: The optimal objective value and the optimal vertex both remain unchanged.
distractors.misconception: the objective changes by the shift times the variable's value

distractors.text: The solution moves immediately to an adjacent vertex of the region.
distractors.misconception: the vertex only changes outside the range

distractors.text: The shadow prices of all constraints remain exactly the same.
distractors.misconception: shadow prices depend on the costs of basic variables

distractors.text: The variable becomes nonbasic and its value drops to zero.
distractors.misconception: this happens only outside the range

distractors.text: The shadow prices increase by exactly the same amount as the cost coefficient.
distractors.misconception: the change in shadow prices is not one for one

explanation: Inside the range the basis is still optimal, so the primal solution is unchanged; the value $c^\top x$ and the shadow prices adapt.

stem: In a maximisation LP, what does the reduced cost of a nonbasic variable tell you?
correct: How much its coefficient must improve before entering the basis pays.
Net gain per unit if it were forced into the solution.

distractors.text: The amount of the variable that appears in the optimal solution.
distractors.misconception: nonbasic variables are zero

distractors.text: The shadow price of the constraint that the variable uses.
distractors.misconception: confuses reduced cost with shadow price

distractors.text: The total cost of producing the optimal quantity of that variable.
distractors.misconception: confuses reduced cost with production cost

distractors.text: The slack of the associated dual constraint is always strictly positive.
distractors.misconception: zero is possible for alternative optima

distractors.text: It is the amount the variable would take if the resource were doubled.
distractors.misconception: reduced cost is not a quantity of the variable

explanation: The reduced cost is $c_j-y^\top a_j$ (for max, non-positive at optimality); it measures the change in the objective per unit of forcing it in.

stem: A new activity with column $a$ and objective coefficient $c$ is proposed for a maximisation LP with optimal shadow prices $y$. When is it worth adding to the production plan?
correct: When its reduced cost $c-y^\top a$ is positive, so it beats its resource cost.
Its value exceeds the shadow-price value of resources used.

distractors.text: Whenever its objective coefficient $c$ is positive, whatever resources it uses.
distractors.misconception: ignores the resources it consumes

distractors.text: Only when its coefficient exceeds those of all existing activities.
distractors.misconception: compares coefficients without resource costs

distractors.text: Whenever its column $a$ has only non-negative entries.
distractors.misconception: the sign of the column alone says nothing about value

distractors.text: Only when all the shadow prices are equal to zero.
distractors.misconception: zero shadow prices would mean free resources

distractors.text: When the new activity is cheaper than all existing activities.
distractors.misconception: comparing coefficients without resource values is not a test

explanation: Pricing out the new column with the current shadow prices shows whether it can improve the objective; if $c-y^\top a\le0$ the plan is still optimal.

stem: What does the max-flow min-cut theorem state?
correct: The maximum $s$-$t$ flow equals the minimum capacity among all possible $s$-$t$ cuts.
A maximum flow has the value of a cheapest cut.

distractors.text: The maximum flow equals the capacity of the largest cut separating $s$ and $t$.
distractors.misconception: confuses minimum with maximum

distractors.text: The maximum flow equals the smallest single edge capacity in the network.
distractors.misconception: ignores the combination of edges in a cut

distractors.text: The maximum flow equals the sum of all edge capacities in the network.
distractors.misconception: many edges are not saturated by a flow

distractors.text: The maximum flow always equals the number of edge-disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$.
distractors.misconception: holds only when all capacities are one

distractors.text: The maximum flow equals the capacity of the cut with the fewest edges.
distractors.misconception: the number of edges in a cut is irrelevant

explanation: Any flow is at most any cut's capacity, and at optimality some cut is saturated, so the two values coincide.

stem: How can you recognise a maximum flow using the residual network?
correct: A flow is maximal exactly when the residual network has no path from $s$ to $t$.
No augmenting path remains in the residual graph of the flow.

distractors.text: The flow is maximal when every edge of the network is saturated.
distractors.misconception: it is enough that one cut is saturated

distractors.text: The flow is maximal when all edges leaving $s$ have a positive flow.
distractors.misconception: positive flow does not ensure optimality

distractors.text: The flow is maximal when no path from $s$ to $t$ exists in the original network.
distractors.misconception: the original network has a path whenever there is any flow

distractors.text: The flow is maximal whenever flow conservation holds at every internal node.
distractors.misconception: conservation holds for all feasible flows

distractors.text: The flow is maximal when the residual network contains a cycle through $s$.
distractors.misconception: cycles do not matter; paths from $s$ to $t$ do

explanation: An augmenting path in the residual network can increase the flow; when none exists, the set reachable from $s$ defines a minimum cut.

stem: All edge capacities of a flow network are integers. Which statement is guaranteed?
correct: Some maximum flow has an integer value on every edge.
An integer-valued maximum flow always exists.

distractors.text: Every maximum flow has integer values on all edges.
distractors.misconception: a maximum flow can split fractionally between equal paths

distractors.text: The maximum flow is integral only if the network has no cycles.
distractors.misconception: acyclicity is not required

distractors.text: An integer maximum flow exists only when all capacities equal one.
distractors.misconception: the integrality theorem covers all integer capacities

distractors.text: The maximum flow value must be an even integer.
distractors.misconception: invents a parity condition

distractors.text: The maximum flow is integral only when the network has a single source and a single sink.
distractors.misconception: integrality does not depend on the number of terminals

explanation: Each augmentation changes the flow by an integer amount (the bottleneck), so Ford-Fulkerson produces integer flows.

stem: What characterises an arbitrage opportunity among currencies with exchange rates $r_{ij}$?
correct: A cycle of conversions with the product of rates above 1.
A cycle of negative weight under $-\log r_{ij}$.

distractors.text: A cycle in which the sum of the exchange rates exceeds the number of currencies.
distractors.misconception: rates multiply rather than add

distractors.text: A cycle whose product of rates is smaller than 1.
distractors.misconception: that loses money

distractors.text: Any cycle of three currencies, whatever the rates.
distractors.misconception: the product of rates must exceed one

distractors.text: A pair of currencies with $r_{ij}=r_{ji}$.
distractors.misconception: consistent rates would rule out arbitrage only when $r_{ij}r_{ji}=1$

distractors.text: A cycle of conversions in which the first and the last currency coincide.
distractors.misconception: every cycle returns to its first currency

explanation: Money is multiplied by each rate along the cycle; taking logs turns the product into a sum, and a negative cycle can be found by Bellman-Ford.

stem: In a minimum cost network flow model, what does the flow conservation constraint at a node say?
correct: Outflow minus inflow equals the node's supply, negative at demand nodes.
Net outflow at a node equals its supply or minus its demand.

distractors.text: Inflow equals outflow at every node of the network, including the supply and demand nodes.
distractors.misconception: ignores the supply and demand nodes

distractors.text: Outflow is at most the cost of the cheapest incident edge.
distractors.misconception: mixes costs into the conservation law

distractors.text: The flow on each edge is at most the supply at its tail.
distractors.misconception: confuses capacity with conservation

distractors.text: Total flow through a node equals its capacity in any feasible solution.
distractors.misconception: a node need not be saturated

distractors.text: The inflow at each node must exceed its outflow by the node's capacity.
distractors.misconception: conservation concerns net supply, not capacity

explanation: Transhipment nodes have zero supply, so inflow equals outflow there; sources and sinks carry the net flow.

stem: For a maximisation integer program, what does the optimal value of its LP relaxation provide?
correct: An upper bound on the optimal value of the integer program.
A value at least as large as the best integer solution.

distractors.text: A lower bound on the optimal value of the integer program.
distractors.misconception: the relaxation enlarges the feasible set, so its maximum is higher

distractors.text: A value that always equals the integer optimum when the data are integers.
distractors.misconception: equality needs special structure

distractors.text: A feasible objective value for the integer program.
distractors.misconception: the relaxation solution may violate integrality

distractors.text: A bound that is valid only when the LP solution is fractional.
distractors.misconception: the bound is always valid

distractors.text: A value equal to the integer optimum if the objective coefficients are integers.
distractors.misconception: integer coefficients do not close the gap

explanation: The relaxation drops integrality, which can only enlarge the feasible set; the maximum over a bigger set is at least as large.

stem: The LP relaxation of an integer program has a fractional optimum. What is the issue with simply rounding it to the nearest integers?
correct: The rounded point may violate a constraint, or it may be far from the true optimum.
Feasibility and optimality of the rounded point are not guaranteed.

distractors.text: The rounded point is always feasible, but never optimal.
distractors.misconception: rounded points can be infeasible and sometimes optimal

distractors.text: It always yields a lower bound that equals the integer optimum.
distractors.misconception: the rounded value need not equal the optimum

distractors.text: It gives the optimum whenever the constraints are all of the less-than-or-equal type.
distractors.misconception: no such guarantee exists

distractors.text: The rounded solution is optimal for the LP relaxation as well.
distractors.misconception: it need not even be feasible for the relaxation

distractors.text: Rounding always gives a point with a better objective value than the relaxation.
distractors.misconception: the relaxation value is the best possible

explanation: Rounding can leave the feasible region (for example, rounding up a tight constraint) and can lose a lot of value.

stem: In branch-and-bound for a maximisation IP, when can a node be pruned?
correct: When infeasible, integral, or no better than the incumbent.
When its upper bound cannot beat the incumbent.

distractors.text: Whenever its LP solution contains a fractional variable.
distractors.misconception: fractional nodes are the ones that need branching

distractors.text: When its LP bound is strictly larger than the incumbent value.
distractors.misconception: such a node may still contain a better solution

distractors.text: As soon as its depth in the tree exceeds the number of variables.
distractors.misconception: depth is not a pruning criterion

distractors.text: When its LP relaxation is unbounded, because that gives a good bound.
distractors.misconception: an unbounded node must be branched or analysed

distractors.text: When its LP bound is below zero, whatever the incumbent is.
distractors.misconception: pruning compares with the incumbent, not with zero

explanation: Pruning is safe when a node cannot contain a solution better than the incumbent: infeasible, integral (record it), or bounded by the incumbent.

stem: In branch-and-bound a variable has the fractional LP value $x_j=3.4$. How are the two child subproblems formed?
correct: One adds the constraint $x_j\le3$, the other adds $x_j\ge4$.
The two child problems are $x_j\le3$ and $x_j\ge4$.

distractors.text: One adds $x_j\le3.4$ and the other adds $x_j\ge3.4$.
distractors.misconception: the current LP solution stays feasible in both

distractors.text: One fixes $x_j=3$ and the other fixes $x_j=4$.
distractors.misconception: all other integer values are lost

distractors.text: One adds $x_j\le4$ and the other adds $x_j\ge3$.
distractors.misconception: the branches overlap and the fractional point remains feasible

distractors.text: One restricts $x_j\le0$ and the other restricts $x_j\ge7$.
distractors.misconception: arbitrary bounds cut off integer solutions

distractors.text: One fixes $x_j$ at the rounded value $3$ and the other drops $x_j$ from the problem.
distractors.misconception: discards integer values of the variable

explanation: Every integer solution satisfies $x_j\le3$ or $x_j\ge4$, but the fractional point $3.4$ satisfies neither branch.

stem: A fixed set-up cost is incurred if product $x$ is made at all. The constraint $x\le My$ with $y\in\{0,1\}$ and a cost $Fy$ is used. What does it model?
correct: If $y=0$ then $x=0$; if $y=1$ then $x\le M$ and $F$ is paid.
The cost $F$ is paid only when production is positive.

distractors.text: If $y=1$ then $x$ must equal $M$ exactly.
distractors.misconception: the constraint is only an upper bound

distractors.text: If $x>0$ then $y$ must be $0$, so the set-up cost is avoided.
distractors.misconception: reverses the logic

distractors.text: Both $x$ and $y$ are binary variables restricted to $0$ or $1$.
distractors.misconception: $x$ is continuous in a fixed-charge model

distractors.text: The constraint forces $x$ to be zero in any optimal solution.
distractors.misconception: $x$ can be positive when $y=1$

distractors.text: The constraint makes $y$ continuous so that set-up costs scale with $x$.
distractors.misconception: $y$ is binary in this construction

explanation: If $x>0$ the constraint forces $y=1$, and minimising cost keeps $y=0$ otherwise; $M$ must be a valid upper bound for $x$.

stem: What property must a valid cutting plane have for an integer program?
correct: All integer feasible points satisfy it, but the fractional LP optimum violates it.
It removes the LP optimum but keeps every integer point.

distractors.text: It is satisfied by the current fractional LP optimum, so the optimum stays feasible.
distractors.misconception: then it does not cut anything off

distractors.text: It removes some feasible integer points to shrink the region faster.
distractors.misconception: that would lose possible optima

distractors.text: It is parallel to the objective function and passes through the optimum.
distractors.misconception: geometry of the objective is unrelated

distractors.text: It has integer coefficients but need not exclude any LP point.
distractors.misconception: an ineffective cut is not a cut

distractors.text: It passes through the LP optimum and cuts off a fraction of the integer points.
distractors.misconception: valid cuts must keep every integer point

explanation: A cut tightens the LP relaxation without losing integer solutions; repeated cuts push the LP optimum towards an integer point.

stem: How is a Gomory fractional cut obtained from a tableau row whose basic variable has a fractional value?
correct: Use the fractional parts of the row and require $\sum_jf_jx_j\ge f_0$ over nonbasic variables.
Weighted nonbasic sum at least the fractional right-hand side.

distractors.text: Take the integer parts of the coefficients and require the sum to be at most the integer part of the right-hand side.
distractors.misconception: uses the integer parts rather than fractional parts

distractors.text: Require $\sum_j f_jx_j\le f_0$ with the fractional parts of the row.
distractors.misconception: reverses the inequality

distractors.text: Use the fractional part of the objective row and set it equal to zero.
distractors.misconception: cuts come from a constraint row, not the objective row

distractors.text: Round every coefficient of the row up to the next integer and keep the equality.
distractors.misconception: rounding does not give a valid cut

distractors.text: Add the constraint that every nonbasic variable equals its integer part.
distractors.misconception: this removes valid integer solutions

explanation: The basic variable equals an integer plus fractions; integrality of the left side forces $\sum f_jx_j$ to be at least $f_0$.

stem: Under which condition is a Gomory fractional cut guaranteed to be valid?
correct: When every slack variable is integer at integer solutions.
With integer data in the constraints.

distractors.text: Only when the problem is a minimisation problem.
distractors.misconception: the validity does not depend on the direction of optimisation

distractors.text: Only when every variable is restricted to be binary.
distractors.misconception: general integers are fine

distractors.text: Only when the LP optimum is degenerate.
distractors.misconception: degeneracy is irrelevant

distractors.text: Only when the objective coefficients are fractional.
distractors.misconception: the argument involves the constraint row, not the objective

distractors.text: Only when the right-hand side of the cut is negative.
distractors.misconception: the right-hand side of a Gomory cut is a fractional part

explanation: The proof uses that the left-hand side of the row is an integer; with fractional data the slack variables need not be integer, and the cut can be invalid.

stem: Valid cuts are added to a maximisation integer program and the LP relaxation is re-solved. How does its optimal value compare?
correct: It does not increase, and it stays at least as large as the integer optimum.
It decreases or stays the same, above the integer optimum.

distractors.text: It increases, since extra constraints give a better bound.
distractors.misconception: more constraints cannot raise a maximum

distractors.text: It may drop below the integer optimum, since cuts remove feasible points.
distractors.misconception: valid cuts keep all integer points

distractors.text: It stays exactly the same after every cut by definition.
distractors.misconception: useful cuts remove the fractional optimum

distractors.text: The relaxation becomes infeasible whenever the integer program has a solution.
distractors.misconception: valid cuts keep integer solutions

distractors.text: It becomes smaller than the integer optimum after enough cuts.
distractors.misconception: valid cuts never cut off the integer optimum

explanation: A valid cut shrinks the relaxation but keeps every integer solution, so the bound tightens but never crosses the integer optimum.

stem: How do linear programming and integer programming compare in computational complexity?
correct: LP is solvable in polynomial time, whereas general integer programming is NP-hard.
Integer programming is NP-hard; LP is polynomial.

distractors.text: Both LP and general integer programming are solvable in polynomial time.
distractors.misconception: underestimates the difficulty of integer programming

distractors.text: Integer programming is polynomial but LP is NP-hard.
distractors.misconception: reverses the two classes

distractors.text: The simplex method is guaranteed to run in polynomial time on every LP.
distractors.misconception: simplex is exponential in the worst case

distractors.text: Integer programming is easy whenever the coefficients are rational numbers.
distractors.misconception: rational data does not remove the hardness

distractors.text: Integer programming reduces to LP by dropping the integrality, with no loss.
distractors.misconception: dropping integrality changes the problem

explanation: Interior-point and ellipsoid methods solve LPs in polynomial time; simplex is fast in practice but exponential in the worst case.

stem: What is the definition of a convex function $f$?
correct: $f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\le\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)$ for all $x$, $y$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$.
The graph of $f$ lies below every chord of the graph.

distractors.text: $f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\ge\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)$ for all such $x,y,\theta$.
distractors.misconception: this is the definition of concave

distractors.text: $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ for all points $x$ and $y$.
distractors.misconception: describes additivity, which is linearity

distractors.text: $f$ has a unique minimiser and is non-negative everywhere.
distractors.misconception: describes a property that follows only for some convex functions

distractors.text: $f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}$ for all such $x,y,\theta$.
distractors.misconception: this is quasiconvexity, which is weaker

distractors.text: $f(x)\le f(y)+\nabla f(y)^\top(x-y)$ for all $x$ and $y$.
distractors.misconception: the reversed tangent inequality characterises concave functions

explanation: Convexity compares the function at a mixture with the mixture of values; the quasiconvex condition is weaker.

stem: A twice continuously differentiable function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. When is $f$ convex?
correct: Its Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point of the domain.
The Hessian has no negative eigenvalue at any point.

distractors.text: Only when its Hessian is positive definite at every point.
distractors.misconception: convex functions such as $x^4$ have a singular Hessian at $0$

distractors.text: Whenever the determinant of the Hessian is positive.
distractors.misconception: two negative eigenvalues also give a positive determinant

distractors.text: Whenever the trace of the Hessian is positive everywhere.
distractors.misconception: a positive trace allows one negative eigenvalue

distractors.text: Whenever all the entries of the Hessian are non-negative.
distractors.misconception: entries alone do not determine definiteness

distractors.text: Whenever its Hessian is symmetric at every point of the domain.
distractors.misconception: symmetry holds for all smooth functions

explanation: Convexity is equivalent to the Hessian being PSD; positive definiteness is sufficient for strict convexity, not necessary.

stem: What is special about a local minimiser of a convex function over a convex set?
correct: It is also a global minimiser of the problem.
No feasible point has a lower objective value.

distractors.text: It is the unique minimiser of the problem.
distractors.misconception: a flat region can contain many minimisers

distractors.text: It must lie on a vertex of the feasible set.
distractors.misconception: convex minimisers can be interior points

distractors.text: It is a KKT point only when the objective is also concave.
distractors.misconception: confuses with concavity

distractors.text: It must lie on the boundary of the feasible set.
distractors.misconception: unconstrained minima are interior

distractors.text: It is a saddle point of the objective in general.
distractors.misconception: local minima of convex functions are not saddle points

explanation: If a better point existed, moving along the segment towards it would lower the objective near the local minimiser, by convexity.

stem: A convex problem with differentiable functions satisfies Slater's condition. What is the status of the KKT conditions?
correct: They are necessary and sufficient for global optimality.
A feasible point is optimal exactly when KKT multipliers exist.

distractors.text: They are sufficient but not necessary for optimality.
distractors.misconception: Slater's condition makes them necessary as well

distractors.text: They are necessary but not sufficient for optimality.
distractors.misconception: convexity gives sufficiency

distractors.text: They are neither necessary nor sufficient unless the objective is linear.
distractors.misconception: linearity is not needed

distractors.text: They are necessary and sufficient only at vertices of the feasible set.
distractors.misconception: the position of the optimum does not matter

distractors.text: They are necessary but their solutions never give the global optimum.
distractors.misconception: for convex problems KKT points are global optima

explanation: Convexity gives sufficiency of KKT, and a constraint qualification such as Slater gives necessity.

stem: What are the basic facts about the Lagrangian dual function $g(\lambda)=\inf_xL(x,\lambda)$ of a primal problem with inequality constraints?
correct: It is concave, and for $\lambda\ge0$ it lower-bounds the primal optimum.
It never exceeds the primal optimum, and is concave.

distractors.text: It is convex in $\lambda$ and an upper bound on the primal optimal value.
distractors.misconception: reverses both convexity and the bound

distractors.text: It is concave but it overestimates the primal optimum for $\lambda\ge0$.
distractors.misconception: gets the bound direction wrong

distractors.text: It equals the primal optimal value for every multiplier $\lambda$.
distractors.misconception: equality needs the optimal multiplier

distractors.text: It is concave only when the primal problem is convex.
distractors.misconception: the dual function is always concave

distractors.text: It is convex in $\lambda$ only when the primal problem is a linear program.
distractors.misconception: concavity holds for any primal problem

explanation: As the infimum of functions affine in $\lambda$, $g$ is concave for any problem; weak duality gives $g(\lambda)\le p^*$.

stem: What does complementary slackness say in the KKT conditions for the constraints $g_i(x)\le0$?
correct: Each multiplier $\lambda_i$ is zero unless its constraint is active.
Each product $\lambda_ig_i(x^*)$ vanishes at the optimum.

distractors.text: Every multiplier is strictly positive at the optimum.
distractors.misconception: inactive constraints have zero multipliers

distractors.text: Each constraint must be violated, $g_i(x^*)>0$, when its multiplier is positive.
distractors.misconception: an active constraint is satisfied with equality

distractors.text: Each multiplier equals the value $g_i(x^*)$ of its constraint.
distractors.misconception: confuses the multiplier with the constraint value

distractors.text: The multipliers must add up to one.
distractors.misconception: confuses with probabilities

distractors.text: The multipliers of the active constraints must all be negative.
distractors.misconception: multipliers of $\le$ constraints are non-negative in a minimisation

explanation: An inactive constraint does not affect the optimum locally, so its multiplier is zero; a positive multiplier forces the constraint to be tight.

stem: A convex quadratic program minimises $\tfrac12x^\top Qx+c^\top x$ subject to linear constraints, with $Q$ positive semidefinite. Where can the minimiser lie?
correct: Anywhere in the feasible set, even in the interior.
At an interior point, on a face, or at a vertex.

distractors.text: Always at a vertex of the feasible polyhedron, as for linear programs.
distractors.misconception: the quadratic term can pull the optimum off the vertices

distractors.text: Only on the boundary of the feasible set.
distractors.misconception: interior minima occur when the unconstrained minimiser is feasible

distractors.text: Only at the origin, because quadratic forms are minimised there.
distractors.misconception: the linear term moves the minimiser

distractors.text: Only where all the constraints hold with equality.
distractors.misconception: constraints may be inactive

distractors.text: Always at a point where the objective gradient is zero.
distractors.misconception: constraints can hold the optimum away from the unconstrained minimiser

explanation: Unlike LP, the objective curves, so a minimiser may be interior or on an edge; convexity makes any KKT point globally optimal.

stem: Fully invested portfolios (weights sum to one, short sales allowed) with covariance matrix $\Sigma$. What is the minimum-variance portfolio?
correct: The weights are proportional to $\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1$, scaled so that they sum to one.
The vector $\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1$ rescaled so that the weights sum to one.

distractors.text: The weights proportional to $\Sigma\mathbf 1$, scaled to sum to one.
distractors.misconception: forgets the inverse of the covariance matrix

distractors.text: The weights inversely proportional to the variances, whatever the correlations.
distractors.misconception: correct only for uncorrelated assets

distractors.text: The equal-weight portfolio, which is optimal for any covariance matrix.
distractors.misconception: equal weights are optimal only in symmetric cases

distractors.text: The weights proportional to the vector of expected returns.
distractors.misconception: ignores risk entirely

distractors.text: The weights proportional to the inverse of each asset's expected return.
distractors.misconception: expected returns do not enter the minimum-variance problem

explanation: The Lagrange condition $\Sigma w=\lambda\mathbf 1$ gives $w\propto\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1$, with minimum variance $1/(\mathbf 1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1)$.

stem: Two risky assets have correlation $\rho<1$. How does the volatility of a 50/50 portfolio compare with the average of their volatilities?
correct: It is strictly smaller than the average of the volatilities.
Combining assets lowers risk below the average risk.

distractors.text: It equals the average of the two volatilities for every $\rho$.
distractors.misconception: holds only when $\rho=1$

distractors.text: It is larger than the average of the volatilities.
distractors.misconception: reverses the diversification effect

distractors.text: It equals the smaller volatility of the two assets.
distractors.misconception: not true in general

distractors.text: It depends only on the expected returns and not on the correlation.
distractors.misconception: risk depends on covariances

distractors.text: It equals the average of the two volatilities whenever the two means are different.
distractors.misconception: confuses means with risk

explanation: With $\rho<1$ the variance is below the squared average volatility, which is the diversification benefit.

stem: What is the efficient frontier in mean-variance analysis?
correct: Least variance for a given expected return, upper branch.
Highest return for a given level of variance.

distractors.text: The set of all feasible portfolios, including dominated ones.
distractors.misconception: the frontier excludes dominated portfolios

distractors.text: The portfolios with the highest Sharpe ratio for every risk level.
distractors.misconception: only the tangency portfolio maximises the Sharpe ratio

distractors.text: The portfolios that have zero variance.
distractors.misconception: risky assets cannot all have zero variance

distractors.text: The equal-weighted portfolios of all subsets of assets.
distractors.misconception: the weights are optimised, not equal

distractors.text: The set of portfolios with maximum variance for each expected return.
distractors.misconception: maximising variance is the opposite of efficiency

explanation: The efficient frontier is the upper part of the minimum-variance curve; portfolios below the minimum-variance point are dominated.

stem: The covariance matrix $\Sigma$ of the assets is singular, for example because one asset is a combination of others. What is the consequence for the minimum-variance problem?
correct: $\Sigma^{-1}$ does not exist, and the minimiser may not be unique.
The objective is not strictly convex.

distractors.text: The portfolio variance can become negative.
distractors.misconception: a covariance matrix is positive semidefinite, so variance is non-negative

distractors.text: The problem becomes non-convex and has no minimiser.
distractors.misconception: it is still a convex QP

distractors.text: The minimum variance is always exactly one.
distractors.misconception: invents a value

distractors.text: Every portfolio has the same variance.
distractors.misconception: singular directions are special, not all

distractors.text: The minimum-variance portfolio is the zero vector of weights.
distractors.misconception: the budget constraint rules out zero weights

explanation: A singular PSD $\Sigma$ has a zero-variance direction; the problem stays convex but the weights are not determined uniquely.

stem: Why may assets be clustered before building a portfolio?
correct: It groups correlated assets, so fewer covariances need estimating.
It stabilises the estimated covariance matrix.

distractors.text: To guarantee a higher expected return than any unclustered portfolio.
distractors.misconception: clustering gives no return guarantee

distractors.text: To make the covariance matrix exactly diagonal.
distractors.misconception: clusters remain correlated

distractors.text: To eliminate all systematic risk from the portfolio.
distractors.misconception: systematic risk cannot be clustered away

distractors.text: To make the weights sum to one automatically.
distractors.misconception: unrelated to the budget constraint

distractors.text: To remove any need for estimating expected returns in the model.
distractors.misconception: clustering does not remove the estimation of returns

explanation: With many assets the sample covariance matrix is noisy; grouping similar assets lets one allocate across groups first.
